practice.title: Three-Step Meditation Practice
agreedSteps: Transforming Adversity meditation — Purpose: to help us overcome our chosen delusion by transforming all obstacles into part of the path. Object: a determination to transform everything that comes along into an opportunity to advance our practice. Actual meditation: admire the good qualities that come from transforming adversity.

Five Benefits of Bodhichitta (Nimku) meditation — Purpose: to strengthen our bodhisattva vow and resolve. Object: a feeling of happiness and rejoicing at having taken the bodhisattva vows. Actual meditation: go through the five benefits — supreme nectar overcoming death, inexhaustible treasury, supreme medicine, shady tree, universal bridge — and admire what bodhichitta can accomplish.
steps: Consider: how particular am I? Can I let go of needing conditions to be a certain way in order to be happy?
Practice the mantra throughout the day: 'I don't need it to be this way or that way. What I really need to do is transform my mind.'

When something unexpected arises, ask for wisdom blessings to see the condition as favorable — this is especially Dorje Shugden's function, blessing our mind to see every condition as part of our path.

Reflect on the 0-to-100 scale of wishing faith: how strong is my wish to overcome my chosen delusion? If we're not seeing obvious movement, it's worth assuming our wish is about a 5 and looking at how to raise it through admiring and believing faith.
practice.quote: I don't need things to be this way or that way. What I really need to do is transform my mind and oppose my delusions, my real obstacles.

commentary.title: Three-Step Meditation
content: How is our meditation going? Are we meditating according to Geshe Kelsang's tradition — using analytical meditation to find the object, then doing placement meditation on it? Even more precisely, the way the lamrim meditations are structured in Mirror of Dharma with Additions is: the purpose, the object, and the actual meditation.

The purpose is the why — it gives us the buy-in. It gives us wishing faith and admiring faith in what we're actually doing. The object clarifies what specific insight or determination the meditation is leading to, so we actually know where we're going. And the actual meditation is the analytical contemplation — what we think about to arrive at that object.

For example, in the bodhisattva vow meditation we did at the start of class: the purpose is that we attain enlightenment through taking and keeping the bodhisattva vows. The object is a strong determination to take and keep those vows. The actual meditation is considering the benefits we get from taking and keeping the vows, and why that's necessary to attain enlightenment.

The lamrim meditations in Mirror of Dharma with Additions already have these three parts clearly laid out — Geshe Kelsang called it the best presentation of how to meditate. But when we're working with other teachings or applying Dharma to our personal delusion project, we need to extract the structure ourselves: what's the purpose, what's the object, what's the actual meditation? The actual meditation distills the purpose into its essential contemplation — the specific thoughts we use in analytical meditation to arrive at the object.

We should always be thinking this way — what's the practice here? How am I going to take these Dharma teachings and turn them into an experience in my life? And if we teach meditation, we should prepare our classes this way too. The discipline of trying to identify these three parts makes the class way better, and it's also humbling — sometimes we realize we have no idea what spiritual experience we're trying to lead people toward.
commentary.quote: That's the way a practitioner thinks — [...] how am I going to take this information, these Dharma teachings, and turn them into an experience in my life?

commentary.title: Rejoicing in Bodhichitta
content: Once we have developed the precious bodhichitta, we should be full of praise and encouragement, uplifting ourselves with joy: 'Now my life has borne great fruit. My human life has attained great meaning.' Verses 26 and 27 are famous — we recite them in various bodhisattva vow ceremonies.

These words are very melodic and beautiful and easy to learn. They're lovely to recite in the morning when we retake our bodhisattva vows. We can feel like we got knighted a bodhisattva — we're part of something very noble and special, and we're going to do it right. We're going to really respect this privilege that we've been given in this life.

There's something important here that we might not all be aware of: the feeling of happiness when we take a vow is actually part of taking the vow. That little blissful, happy feeling — that's really when we've taken it. That's why it's included in the various vow ceremonies, where we say, 'Now be happy that you've taken the vow.' That happiness is kind of like locking it in.
commentary.quote: [This] feeling of happiness when we take a vow is actually part of taking the vow. [...] That happiness — feeling that happiness — is kind of like locking it in.

commentary.title: Bodhichitta's Unique Power
content: Developing bodhichitta has a deterministic relationship with enlightenment — that's the key point being raised here. There are lots of other qualities we can develop that don't guarantee we attain enlightenment. We can invest lots of time and lifetimes even developing lots of other qualities, but have nothing to show for it.

In many previous lives we have developed miracle powers and clairvoyance, but where are those powers now? What benefit have they brought any of us? Everything is changing and we are still caught up in the round of samsara. However, if we had previously developed the thought of bodhichitta and engaged in its practices, by now we might have gained the enlightenment of Buddhahood.

Bodhichitta is just the best kind of strategic investment in our time — the best quality that is guaranteed to pay out in the long run. Nothing else fits the bill in the same way. We can feel like we're finally focusing on the one checkpoint that's going to guarantee we move to enlightenment.
commentary.quote: Developing bodhichitta has [...] a deterministic relationship with enlightenment. [...] It's just the best kind of strategic investment in our time.

commentary.title: Building the Foundation
content: Imagine we were all in a race to build a structure as high as a 50-story building. We could do some things that get us far ahead in the lead — get a bunch of metal poles and have them be really tall. At first it would look like we're ahead with ten stories of a pole popping up into the sky. But at some point it's going to topple over from its own weight. There's no firm foundation to hold it up.

That's what practicing higher methods without bodhichitta is like. Without that foundation, we'll be completely unable to practice the tantric path properly. Anyone who practices tantra solely for the sake of benefiting this life is like a person who uses banknotes to light a cigarette, or a Rolls-Royce to cart manure.

What we actually need is a huge foundation — and if we see building projects, they dig really deep into the ground first. The lamrim is designed with this exact understanding in mind. It might look superfluous — why do I have to keep doing meditations on death over and over again? But at some point we'll realize each step is an absolute necessity to go further in the spiritual path.
commentary.quote: You could [...] get a bunch of metal poles and have them be really tall, and at first it would look like — wow, I'm ahead, I've got ten stories of a metal pole popping up into the sky — but at some point you're not going to get to 50 stories. It's going to topple over from its own weight.

commentary.title: Five Benefits (Nimku)
content: Bodhichitta is like supreme nectar that overcomes the great power of death, leading all sentient beings to the eternal state of complete Buddhahood. It is an inexhaustible treasury that eliminates the poverty of all sentient beings by satisfying all their wishes through Dharma teachings and material gifts. It is supreme medicine that relieves all mental and physical sickness.

Just as a shady tree provides refreshment for a tired traveler, bodhichitta provides shade and rest for exhausted sentient beings wandering along the paths of samsara. And it is a universal bridge leading beings from the suffering of the lower realms to the happiness of the higher realms, and ultimately to Buddhahood.

These aren't just poetic metaphors — they describe actual functions of bodhichitta. But the power of enlightened beings is like an iron hook, and for us to be pulled up from our own suffering, we must make a connection with this hook by our own ring of faith. If we do not turn our mind to the Three Jewels, there is no way for them to help us. The causes for our release are not yet complete.

commentary.title: Faith as a Tool
content: Every one of us has chosen a delusion to work on. But what role is faith playing in our destruction of that delusion? Often the issue is that we just don't have a sufficient wish to abandon it. We have a little bit of a wish, but not a wish that's bigger than our wish to do other things. And a wish that's not bigger than our wish to do other things is utterly inert.

We can think of wishing faith on a scale of 0 to 100. Unless we're seeing very obvious movement and inspiration around destroying our delusion, it's helpful to assume it's about a 5. Compare that to things like sleep — somewhere around a 40 or 50, a non-negotiable intention. Or survival — somewhere in the 80s and 90s. That survival mechanism is a really powerful wish.

Often when we're trying to make personal change in spiritual practice, we're trying to make it with a 2 out of 100 level wish. It's a very weak wish that doesn't last and runs out of steam very quickly. But getting rid of our delusions is even more important than survival. The antidote is admiring and believing faith — admire the benefits of freedom from the delusion, believe it's possible, and a wishing faith will arise like a beautiful flower.
commentary.quote: Often when we're trying to make any personal change in spiritual practice, we're trying to make it with a 2 out of 100 level wish, which is a very weak wish. And it's a wish that doesn't last.

commentary.title: Not Being Particular
content: Ask ourselves: how particular am I? I like it this way, but not that way. A bodhisattva's mind is totally open and flexible, thinking about emptiness and benefiting people. It's not that different being here or there, doing this or that. They understand it's all coming from the mind anyway.

Our particularity has created this landmine universe. We have this narrow particular path that we're trying to live on, juxtaposing it to the rest of the world, which in our mind is full of obstacles we have to avoid and control. That mind is very tight and fearful. There's a very close connection between being particular and being fearful — it's an anxious mind that wants to control everything and can't handle uncertainty, change, and variability.

The first step is playing around with this thought throughout the day: I don't need it to be this way or that way — all I need to do is transform my mind. We'll notice a relaxing calm that sets in, an anxiety that melts off. It doesn't mean we don't have a preference, but our happiness isn't linked to it anymore. Having a preference isn't the problem — it's the attachment to the preference.
commentary.quote: [Our particularity has] created this landmine universe. [...] There's a very close connection between being particular and being fearful.

commentary.title: Transforming Obstacles
content: We all know the teachings on transforming adversity, but how often, when adversity strikes, do we think 'good'? Versus how often do we try to control it, resist it, and change it? The adversity in our life is really helping us become more flexible and get out of that particular mind.

There are no inherently existent obstacles. None of them are obstacles from their own side — it's just a matter of how we see them. We have to take a hundred percent of the responsibility for the view that something is an obstacle. The very act of viewing something as an obstacle is the biggest determination that it functions like one.

What we're asking for is a blessing — not for the obstacle to go away, but to not see it as an obstacle, to see it as part of our path. This is especially Dorje Shugden's function: he blesses our mind to see every condition as favorable for our practice. It's like those chaos engineers at Netflix who deliberately create random problems to test the system's adaptability — the chaos of our life is very useful. The more that comes, as long as we're open to learning and training on it, the faster we're going to grow.
commentary.quote: There are no inherent obstacles. [...] It's just a matter of how we see them. We need to ask for wisdom blessings.
